Vs.

full_judgment: 13. The learned trial Court found as a matter of fact that the house in question is not a dwelling house of the Tahbildar family and in arriving at such a finding he relied on Exhibit 'Ka' through which the defendant petitioner purchased the share in the suit property and it is clear from the description given in the sale deed that the property is described as দোকানঘর. Moreover, the trial Court found on a perusal of the materials and evidence on record that the building in question was never used by the Tahbildar family as their residence. There is no evidence at all to show that any member of the Tahbildar family ever lived in the house and it is found after the construction of the building they let it out to different tenants and with that finding the learned trial Court observed that a house which has not actually been used by the undivided family for a number of years is not a dwelling house. It is true that the learned trial Court without going through the decisions simply by relying on the commentaries made in the book 'Law on Partition' published by DLR arrived at such a finding, but I have myself gone through the relevant decisions and it appears that the view taken by the trial Court is absolutely correct. The judicial view is that the expression 'dwelling house belonging to an undivided family', in fact, refers to the family dwelling house. It does not mean any house or building for human dwelling belonging to an undivided family. In the instant case there is no evidence to the effect that it was a family dwelling house but it transpires from evidence that the building was always in the occupation of the tenants. It, thus, appears that the learned trial Court rightly observed that the property in question is, therefore, not a dwelling house belonging to an undivided family within the meaning of section 4 of' the Partition Act. In the case reported in AIR 1953 (Pat) 344. it has been observed that the expression 'dwelling house belonging to an undivided family' in section 4(1) refers to the family dwelling house and not to any house or building for human dwelling belonging to an undivided family. Thus a house which is in the occupation of tenants cannot be said to be family dwelling house. In the instant case the trial Court on consideration of the materials and' evidence on record found that the building in question was never used by the undivided Tahbildar family as their dwelling house and in that view of the materials, section 4 of the Partition Act has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the instant case. It, thus, appears that finding of the trial Court that the defendant petitioner does not answer the description of a member of an undivided family as contemplated in section 4 of the Partition Act nor the property in question has ever been used as a dwelling house by the original owners, namely, Tahbildar family, is backed by evidence and materials on record. In this connection we may also refer to the decision reported in AIR 1950 (Cal) 111 wherein it has been observed by the Calcutta High Court that 'undivided family' means simply a family not divided qua the dwelling house; in other words, a family which owns a dwelling house and has not divided it. The essence of the matter is that the house itself should be undivided amongst the members of the family who are its owners. The emphasis is really on the house which imparts to the family its character of an undivided family. I, therefore, do not find any illegality in the impugned order.
